section.heading: 2.4 Partitioned Matrices
section.paragraph: A key feature of our work with matrices has been the ability to regard a matrix $$A$$ as a list of column vectors rather than just a rectangular array of numbers. This point of view has been so useful that we wish to consider other partitions of $$A$$ , indicated by horizontal and vertical dividing rules, as in Example 1 below. Partitioned matrices appear in most modern applications of linear algebra because the notation highlights essential structures in matrix analysis, as in the chapter introductory example on aircraft design. This section provides an opportunity to review matrix algebra and use the Invertible Matrix Theorem.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: When a matrix $$A$$ appears in a mathematical model of a physical system such as an electrical network, a transportation system, or a large corporation, it may be natural to regard $$A$$ as a partitioned matrix. For instance, if a microcomputer circuit board consists mainly of three VLSI (very large-scale integrated) microchips, then the matrix for the circuit board might have the general form

image.alt: The figure illustrates a 3 by 3 partitioned matrix.

example.paragraph: The submatrices on the “diagonal” of $$A$$ —namely $$A_{11}$$ , $$A_{22}$$ , and $$A_{33}$$ —concern the three VLSI chips, while the other submatrices depend on the interconnections among those microchips.

section.heading: Addition and Scalar Multiplication
section.paragraph: If matrices $$A$$ and $$B$$ are the same size and are partitioned in exactly the same way, then it is natural to make the same partition of the ordinary matrix sum $$A + B$$ . In this case, each block of $$A + B$$ is the (matrix) sum of the corresponding blocks of $$A$$ and $$B$$ . Multiplication of a partitioned matrix by a scalar is also computed block by block.
section.heading: Multiplication of Partitioned Matrices
section.paragraph: Partitioned matrices can be multiplied by the usual row–column rule as if the block entries were scalars, provided that for a product $$A B$$ , the column partition of $$A$$ matches the row partition of $$B$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let

image.alt: The figure illustrates two matrices of orders 3 by 5 and 5 by 2 partitioned into submatrices of distinct orders.

example.paragraph: The $$5$$ columns of $$A$$ are partitioned into a set of $$3$$ columns and then a set of $$2$$ columns. The $$5$$ rows of $$B$$ are partitioned in the same way—into a set of $$3$$ rows and then a set of $$2$$ rows. We say that the partitions of $$A$$ and $$B$$ are conformable for block multiplication. It can be shown that the ordinary product $$A B$$ can be written as

image.alt: The figure illustrates matrix product A B obtained by multiplying the partitioned matrices A and B.

example.paragraph: It is important for each smaller product in the expression for $$A B$$ to be written with the submatrix from $$A$$ on the left, since matrix multiplication is not commutative. For instance,

$$A_{11} B_{1} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 & - 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 & - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}6 & 4 \\ - 2 & 1 \\ - 3 & 7\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}15 & 1 2 \\ 2 & - 5\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} A_{12} B_{2} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 4 \\ 3 & - 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 1 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 20 & - 8 \\ - 8 & 7\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$
Hence the top block in $$A B$$ is
$$A_{11} B_{1} + A_{12} B_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 1 2 \\ 2 & - 5 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} - 20 & - 8 \\ - 8 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - 5 & 4 \\ - 6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

section.paragraph: The row–column rule for multiplication of block matrices provides the most general way to regard the product of two matrices. Each of the following views of a product has already been described using simple partitions of matrices: (1) the definition of $$A\textbf{x}$$ using the columns of $$A$$ , (2) the column definition of $$A B$$ , (3) the row–column rule for computing $$A B$$ , and (4) the rows of $$A B$$ as products of the rows of $$A$$ and the matrix $$B$$ . A fifth view of $$A B$$ , again using partitions, follows in Theorem 10.

The calculations in the next example prepare the way for Theorem 10. Here $$\text{Col} _{k}(A)$$ is the $$k \text{th}$$ column of $$A$$ , and $$\text{row} _{k}(B)$$ is the $$k \text{th}$$ row of $$B$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} {- 3} & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & {- 4} & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$B = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \\ e & f \end{bmatrix}$$ . Verify that

$$A B = \text{col} _{1} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \text{row} _{1} \left(\right. B \left.\right) + \text{col} _{2} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \text{row} _{2} \left(\right. B \left.\right) + \text{col} _{3} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \text{row} _{3} \left(\right. B \left.\right)$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Each term in the preceding equation is an outer product. (See Exercises 35 and 36 in Section 2.1.) By the row–column rule for computing a matrix product,

$$\text{col} _{1} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \text{row} _{1} \left(\right. B \left.\right) & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a & b\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 a & - 3 b \\ a & b\end{matrix} \left]\right. \text{col} _{2} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \text{row} _{2} \left(\right. B \left.\right) & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ - 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}c & d\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}c & d \\ - 4 c & - 4 d\end{matrix} \left]\right. \text{col} _{3} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \text{row} _{3} \left(\right. B \left.\right) & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 5\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}e & f\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 e & 2 f \\ 5 e & 5 f\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
Thus
$$\sum_{k = 1}^{3} \text{col} _{k} \left(A\right) \text{row} _{k} \left(B\right) = \begin{bmatrix} - 3 a + c + 2 e & - 3 b + d + 2 f \\ a - 4 c + 5 e & b - 4 d + 5 f \end{bmatrix}$$

This matrix is obviously $$A B$$ . Notice that the $$(1,1)$$ -entry in $$A B$$ is the sum of the $$(1,1)$$ -entries in the three outer products, the $$(1,2)$$ -entry in $$A B$$ is the sum of the $$(1,2)$$ -entries in the three outer products, and so on.

note.heading: Theorem 10
Column–Row Expansion of AB
note.paragraph: If $$A$$ is $$m \times n$$ and $$B$$ is $$n \times p$$ , then

$$A B & = & \left[ \text{col} _{1} ( A ) \text{col} _{2} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \hdots \text{col} _{n} \left(\right. A \left.\right)\right] \left[\right. \begin{matrix} \text{row} _{1} \left(\right. B \left.\right) \\ \text{row} _{2} \left(\right. B \left.\right) \\ \vdots \\ \text{row} _{n} \left(\right. B \left.\right)\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \text{col} _{1} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \text{row} _{1} \left(\right. B \left.\right) + \hdots + \text{col} _{n} \left(\right. A \left.\right) \text{row} _{n} \left(\right. B \left.\right)$$

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: For each row index $$i$$ and column index $$j$$ , the $$(i,j) \text{-entry}$$ in $$\text{col} _{k}(A) \text{row} _{k}(B)$$ is the product of $$a_{ik}$$ from $$\text{col} _{k}(A)$$ and $$b_{kj}$$ from $$\text{row} _{k}(B)$$ Hence the $$(i,j) \text{-entry}$$ in the sum shown in equation (1) is
$$a_{i 1} b_{1 j} & + & a_{i 2} b_{2 j} & + & \hdots & + & a_{i n} b_{n j} \left(\right. k = 1 \left.\right) & & \left(\right. k = 2 \left.\right) & & & & \left(\right. k = n \left.\right)$$
This sum is also the $$(i,j) \text{-entry}$$ in $$A B$$ , by the row–column rule.

section.paragraph: A block diagonal matrix is a partitioned matrix with zero blocks off the main diagonal (of blocks). Such a matrix is invertible if and only if each block on the diagonal is invertible. See Exercises 15 and 16.

list.item: When matrices are too large to fit in a computer’s high-speed memory, partitioning permits the computer to work with only two or three submatrices at a time. For instance, one linear programming research team simplified a problem by partitioning the matrix into $$837$$ rows and $$51$$ columns. The problem’s solution took about $$4$$ minutes on a Cray supercomputer.1﻿
Some high-speed computers, particularly those with vector pipeline architecture, perform matrix calculations more efficiently when the algorithms use partitioned matrices.2
Professional software for high-performance numerical linear algebra, such as LAPACK, makes intensive use of partitioned matrix calculations.

section.paragraph: The exercises that follow give practice with matrix algebra and illustrate typical calculations found in applications.
